Sources indicate that in my eyes, the best gift is a practical one. It’s useful and won’t rot in the back of someone’s closet for years; they’ll think of you whenever they use it; and you get major brownie points for introducing a magical, miracle product into their life. And what’s better than being known as someone who reliably gifts reliable products? I may still get made fun of by family for my history of wanting practical gifts (including lead refills for my mechanical pencil), but the gifts I treasure most often get the most use in my home. If you know someone automating their smart home, we’ve got a separate guide for that. But if you’re looking for purpose-driven products, below you’ll find some of the best practical gear to give to friends and family members who value utilitarianism over flash and fluff.

According to recent reports, the OLIGHT Baton4 Pro rechargeable flashlight is a $63 flashlight that’s well worth the cost. They’ll never need another flashlight, and they’ll struggle to find one as bright and powerful as this. This torch clocks in at 1600 lumens, and its beam reaches 200 meters long, with a cool white color that cuts through the darkest sky. Dual switches—a side switch and tail switch—allow for one-handed mode selection (choose from high, turbo, and momentary on). Use it hands-free with an included L stand that sticks to metal surfaces, and know it will stay cool and comfortable in hand, even in Turbo mode. Charge it with the included magnetic charger, or unscrew the tailcap to reveal a USB-C port for universal charging anywhere. Your next power outage, camping trip, and attic exploration mission will thank you for this gift.

Carry an entire box’s worth of tools in your hand with this $130 LEATHERMAN Wave Plus 18-in-1 Multi-Tool. Standouts and crowd-pleasers include regular pliers, needle-nose pliers, replaceable wire cutters, knives, a saw, a can opener, a bottle opener, spring-action scissors, and three driver sizes. This multitool is made to be portable, reliable, durable, and multifunctional, all ingredients for one practical gift.

Made from 100 percent Greek Koroneiki olives, this single-varietal, cold-extracted, early harvest extra virgin olive oil adds zest to whatever you love best. From a bowl of simple greens to artisan bread, grilled fish to wood-fired vegetables, you’ll love the grassy, sassy brightness it brings. And that’s how you also know it’s packed with plenty of polyphenols, so you can fight free radicals—reducing inflammation while elevating taste. Combine it with basil and black olives for the kind of flavor the foodies in your life will want to put on a pedestal (not included) … just one of the many kitchen gifts we can recommend.

It has been revealed that being backstage at a show is a vibe. Sometimes weird, sometimes wild, but always an interesting mix of calm and chaos. Chicago’s FRET12 brand aims to capture the smell of decompression and anticipation and bring it home with its hand-poured “Green Room” candle, which blends birch, bark, fig, and bergamot into something restful and ripe you can gift the joint audiophile-aromaphile in your orbit. For something more after-hours and intimate, try “Deep Cuts,” or spark up “Campfire Acoustic” and bask in wafts of sweet, warm smoke and vanilla. Available in 3-, 8-, and 10-ounce sizes. And while you’re at it, pick up a custom-designed and -printed T-shirt and other garb for that special member of your personal road crew who wants to celebrate their love of all things analog while they shop for some M&M’s (no brown ones) and white tube socks. And there’s artwork and actual guitar stuff, too, for gigging musicians!

Industry observers note that the Mileseey GeneSonic Pro and GenePro G1 give you what you want for a casual round with friends, and what you need if you still want to know that carry number or feel confident before you even swing a club in more serious competition. The IP65 GenePro G1 delivers accuracy on par with top-of-the-line rangefinders on the market today, while also giving you a full view of the hole. It offers front/center/back yardages, Ball-to-Pin distance, 600-yard flag-lock, SmartSlope compensation, and more. And the IP67 magnetically mounted GeneSonic Pro speaker delivers quality sound and a built-in detachable GPS with 43,000+ preloaded advanced course views for those pesky cart path-only days. Plus, it’s a 30W power bank, so you can get out and continue to jam out, no matter what the weather brings or how you swing. Whichever one suits your game, you can’t go wrong, and they make a great gift for the golfer in your life.

If you’re looking to give a gift that no one asks for but nearly everybody needs, four new tires is something someone you know has been putting off. If you know someone with a pickup, SUV, or van that is constantly on the road in mixed conditions, including snow, you can show you care about their safety with four Kumho Road Venture HT tires [left, above]. They come with a 75,000-mile tread warranty on passenger sizes (50,000 on LT sizes), so this is something they won’t have to think about again for years. The zig-zag tread and 3D interlocking sipes earn these a Three-Peak Mountain Snowflake, which means they beat a standard tire’s acceleration on medium-packed snow by at least 10 percent. Meanwhile, four deep grooves channel water away when rain is the bigger problem, and staggered tread blocks mean less highway hum in general. If you know a driver going everywhere (except off-road), you’ll be giving them smoother rides on a road trip, fewer white-knuckle mornings (even in January), and no tire talk for a while. Having taken them out on a closed course near Seattle, we can confirm good dry grip, even during aggressive cornering, and well-composed wet performance. No, they might not unwrap these and squeal … but with fresh tread, these tires shouldn’t squeal either, and that’s something to get excited about. If the person you’re gifting is an SUV or crossover driver more interested in a quiet, plush ride over snow grip, the Crugen GT Pro [right, above], packed with resonance-reduction tech, offers less wheel slip under hard acceleration, strong hydroplaning resistance, and consistent cabin quietness compared to whatever bald rubber they’ve been riding on for too long.

Sources indicate that I’ve sung the praises of this $98 Levoit Core300-P air purifier for years. It’s one of our best budget air purifiers, and there are right now two of them in my home: one in the primary bedroom and another in the living room. The replaceable filters aren’t prohibitively expensive, and they’re whisper-quiet at their lowest speeds. I’ve tested many air purifiers, and this one easily beats its more expensive competitors. My asthmatic cat loves this air purifier, my fiancé, who hasn’t gotten sick in years, loves it, and I love it. I’d buy it for all my friends if I could.

Good things come in small packages, including this $180 Midea dehumidifier, which is two feet high and a little over a foot wide. This small dehumidifier holds 3.2 gallons of water and can cover 1,500 square feet, making it perfect for apartments, bathrooms, and even damp walk-in closets. Control it via app or voice, or use the built-in buttons. A side window shows when it’s time to empty the water tank, and a handle makes it easy to carry. The dehumidifier is also on wheels, so you don’t even have to carry it in some cases.

According to recent reports, other humidifiers quickly get gross and grody. The Carepod One is a splurge at $279, but this high-end humidifier stays mold-free thanks to a sterilizable, dishwasher-safe stainless steel basin. It has only three parts to clean: the white wand, stainless steel water tank, and stainless steel inner lid. The humidifier runs for up to 30 hours and includes a built-in timer for hassle-free use. It’s Restriction of Hazardous Substances-certified, meaning it’s free of hazardous substances like lead and mercury.

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, a mess isn’t messy enough to warrant breaking out the major, heavy vacuum, and there is no other pleasure like having a tool for a very specific task. This $80 handheld vacuum from Shark is excellent for cleaning pet hair off couches or collecting the crust from your car. An extra-large dust cup means you can clean all these small messes in one go or have extra room for pet hair when the couch gets particularly fuzzy.

According to recent reports, regardless of water bottle allegiance, the $20 Kuppy Silicone Water Bottle Drying Rack helps reusable bottles of all sizes, wine glasses, and even silicone snack bags dry thoroughly to prevent odor from trapped water. They’re stackable for storage in the water bottle section of a kitchen (Everyone has a Water Bottle Kingdom somewhere in their home). Best of all, they take up less space than traditional dish racks.

Sources indicate that this $37 Aquabliss SF100 Daily Revitalize Shower Filter is for the person in your life who has a codependent relationship with their Brita pitcher. This budget shower filter fits standard fittings and works with fixed, rain, handheld, and combination shower heads. It also adds three to four inches to an existing shower arm and maintains water pressure for cleaner water without weaker streams. The filter cartridge takes two minutes to replace and lasts three to six months depending on water quality.

The Philips Sonicare Prestige 9900 is a $380 rechargeable toothbrush that provides dentist-level cleaning every day. Sonic technology and multi-angle bristles remove plaque regardless of brush technique. SenseIQ Technology automatically adjusts intensity and flashes when it detects too much pressure. This toothbrush comes with five modes, plus three intensity levels. The Oral-B iO Series 3 Rechargeable Electric Toothbrush is a cheaper option that’s still just as giftable.

A water flosser is the bedrock of a well-rounded oral care routine. The Waterpik Aquarius Countertop Water Flosser is a $100 countertop water flosser that’s more like a power washer for mouths. Choose from 10 settings for extra pearly whites, including a massage mode that helps stimulate gums. Although it’s not a replacement for floss, it’s excellent for getting the job done after a late night. I personally use mine after flossing and add a bit of mouthwash to the reservoir to get fluoride where my teeth need it most.

The Nori Press Travel Steam Iron is a $120 handheld iron that resembles a giant hair straightener. If your gift recipient is like me and has ironed out my polo collars with a hair straightener, this iron should feel familiar. Two heated plates iron the front and back of a garment at once, removing wrinkles without an ironing board. The compact iron also includes a built-in steamer to remove wrinkles from more delicate fabrics. At 14 inches long and weighing a little under 1.5 pounds, it’s packable for clothing emergencies.

Sources indicate that the Dyson Supersonic Nural Hair Dryer is a $450 hair dryer designed to maintain healthy hair and a healthy scalp. It’s also engineered to reduce flakes and shedding and balance hair oils. This smart hair dryer reduces airflow and deactivates the heater when set down; a Hall sensor recognizes each attachment as it’s used and automatically adjusts settings based on the attachment; and intelligent heat control monitors airflow to prevent hair damage. It also dries hair fast, a plus for practical friends who hate going to bed with wet hair.

Your most practical friend is most likely a Virgo or Capricorn. Popular Science’s resident Virgo and Managing Editor, Gear & Commerce, enjoys using this Baldscaper to keep his head smooth without causing physical/emotional damage to himself and his loved ones. Four floating shaver heads contour to the head, face, and body for a smooth shave, cutting it close sans nicks and razor burn. It’s fully waterproof, rinses clean with just water, and can be used wet or dry. A powerful motor and 90-minute battery life cut through coarse hair without dying halfway through a head shave.

The TUSHY Classic 3.0 Bidet is a $124 starter bidet that helps your gift recipient feel cleaner than using toilet paper alone. It includes all materials needed for installation, which takes less than 10 minutes. A Schmutz Shield (actual name for this feature) blocks grime from escaping past the toilet lid, and a self-cleaning nozzle means this bidet won’t cause more cleaning-related headaches your practical friend may experience daily.

Shark makes some of the best cordless vacuums, and this $380 option includes some of our favorite features in a vacuum cleaner, including a MultiFLEX wand that makes it infinitely easier to reach under furniture, a light that reveals missed spots, and Floor Detect technology that adjusts brushroll speed depending on the surface. It also doubles as a handvac and comes with tools for crevices and upholstery. With 50 minutes of runtime, HEPA filtration, and an anti-allergen seal, dust busting won’t involve a sneezing fit.

Give the gift of a fully connected home with the $130 Aeotec Smart Home Hub2, which can be used as a SmartThings Hub and supports Zigbee and Matter Gateway protocols. It’s also compatible with Alexa, Google Assistant, and Wi-Fi. Although it’s not Z-Wave compliant, it offers wider device compatibility and stronger security than some competitors.

Sources indicate that the best electric blankets provide warmth without turning up the thermostat. This $50 electric throw blanket from Westinghouse is reliable and heats evenly. Plus, it protects itself from overheating and includes an auto-off function for peace of mind when a nap strikes. A weighty smart digital controller cycles through six heat settings and a timer up to 10 hours. Throw it in the washing machine and hang it to dry between seasons.

The Rumpl Gametime Puffy is a $100 2-in-1 stadium accessory made for overtime, any time. It packs a full-size 50×70″ insulated blanket into a TPU-laminated storage case featuring an adjustable, removable shoulder strap and an integrated 1-inch insulated foam pad to sit on when you pull the blanket out (and it’s an extra-padded 4” cushion with the blanket in). The shell and case have a PFAS-free water-repellent finish, and the blanket keeps you warm down to 45 degrees, making it great for football games, soccer matches, and club tournaments.

In a recent development, I’ve assembled my fair share of furniture from a multinational home furnishings store, and let’s be real: Sometimes those Allen wrenches don’t cut it. Enter the Greenworks Pro PowerAll 24V Drill Driver and Impact Driver Combo Kit, a $169 bundle that gives you two handy tools for the price of one. The drill driver and impact driver use brushless motors and 24-volt batteries, and run 20% longer than 18- and 20-volt counterparts. It’s compact, lightweight, and easy to use in tight spaces, making it an excellent gift for DIY-minded friends and family.

The $65 Anyday 4-Piece Medium Glass Food Storage system is made for microwaving or cooking directly in the oven, thanks to sturdy borosilicate glass that’s stronger and better resists extreme temperature changes than soft glass. The glass dishware is even freezer-safe. A glass lid prevents splatters in the microwave; lay-flat knobs vent food while cooking or create an airtight seal when it’s time to store any leftovers.

In a recent development, this $160 waterproof, compact carry-all from RUX works like an everyday tote, then converts to a roll-top dry bag to protect against rain and random liquids. It fits a laptop, lunch, and any layers, while internal and external pockets keep keys, a phone, and wallet within reach. Grab it by the handles, or wear it crossbody with the included shoulder strap on a two-hands kind of day. Exterior lash points connect pockets and panels (sold separately) for added storage and organization if your gift recipient desires a gift that keeps on giving.

Practical people definitely have plenty of pen opinions—I know I do. And this $6.50 pack of uniball Jetstream pens is a favorite thanks to its smooth, opaque, quick-drying ink that’s water- and fade-resistant. Choose the .7 millimeter option for a finer line, or the 1 millimeter thickness for those who prefer a more robust script.

My $26 LEUCHTTURM1917 A5 notebook holds my journal ramblings, my to-do lists, and random neurotic notes I need to get out of my head and onto a page. Numbered pages, two page markers, and a blank table of contents help organize all my jumbled thoughts. I personally go for a hardcover notebook with ruled paper, but LEUCHTTURM1917 also sells softcover journals in every color of the rainbow, with square grid ruling, dotted ruling, or blank pages.

Recent findings suggest that the Ember Mug 3 is the latest generation of the popular smart mug that can keep hot drinks at a precise temperature all day long. Each 14 oz mug includes a sliding lid that extends battery life up to three hours on a single charge (it’s 80 minutes without the lid). And a charging coaster recharges your mug after your daily dose of bean juice (or maintains the temperature indefinitely if you keep the mug on it). Customize your preferred temperature in the app, or set it manually with a button on the mug. It’s also top-rack dishwasher safe.

Industry observers note that this $35 leakproof travel mug from BrüMate is for those who don’t mix their coffee with their electronics. A ceramic lining preserves flavor while preventing staining and leftover odors, and triple insulation keeps drinks hot or cold for hours. It’s cup-holder friendly for caffeinating on the go, and a magnetic, OctaLock lid prevents spills while running errands.

In a recent development, the Click & Carry Ergonomic Grocery Bag Carrier Handle & Bag Holder is a $14 gizmo that saves trips and reduces hassle when unloading groceries. It’s gentle on joints, reduces hand strain, and its ergonomic design lowers injury risk. The bag carrier has a 100-pound weight capacity but weighs just under three ounces. The friend who always tests the boundaries of bringing everything inside in one trip will thank you.

Industry observers note that socks are a well-liked practical gift, and this $25 two-pack of merino wool, COOLMAX EcoMade polyester, REPREVE recycled polyester + nylon socks from Gordini uses fine-gauge and ultra-lightweight yarns to keep feet dry and supported with Linear Wicking Channels that move away moisture and Quilted AirForms that distribute shock and cushion impact. These OrbitFit anatomically mapped 3D zones create a purpose-knit performance fit that keeps you comfortable at home, on a walk, or while running or hiking. If cotton socks are on the gift list, we’re fans of the HUE Women’s Mini Crew Sock and the Men’s Casual Ribbed Crew Socks, which are breathable and comfortable.

It has been revealed that the Garmin Venu 4 is a $550 multisport watch that blends style and function. A bright 1.4-inch AMOLED display clearly shows health and fitness stats like sleep tracking and time needed for workout recovery, along with on-screen workouts. A smart wake alarm helps with waking up at an optimal time, and a built-in LED flashlight illuminates dark morning walks. This watch supports running and triathlon, strength training, jet lag recovery, and more. Data-obsessed friends and family members will be pleased with all the numbers and stats they can pull from this watch.

It has been revealed that this $50 OtterBox Symmetry Series Case has protected my iPhone 13 for years: the only blemish is a dent in the aluminum bumper from when I took it out of its case and immediately dropped it on my concrete porch. I’ve learned my lesson and never forgo a phone case. The OtterBox Symmetry Series Case is sleek without being too flimsy and protects without bulk. It’s on my repurchase list and should be on yours, too, especially if you’re looking at one of the newly introduced iPhone 18s.

These newly refreshed noise-canceling headphones from Bose are essential for quiet commutes and tuning out the airport chaos while traveling. Bose makes some of our favorite noise-canceling headphones and earbuds thanks to thoughtful design and helpful tech in each pair. We’re particularly fond of the comfortable pill-shaped earcups, 24-hour battery life, Immersive Audio, QuietControl noise cancellation, and updated ActiveSense Tech to smooth sound spikes in Aware Mode.

According to recent reports, this practical gift is also personal. Every pair of these $249 orthotics from Stride is custom-made from a 3D scan of someone’s foot and a gait video with just their smartphone required, no doctor’s visit necessary. Take a short quiz about pain areas, activity levels, goals, and shoe preferences; provide the digital data; and podiatrists in Germany customize the orthotics and print them on durable TPU (personalized for the recipient) before they arrive at your doorstep in just 10 to 15 days. And they go well beyond arch support. It’s hard to convey the initially odd and then quickly invigorating sensation of an insole that considers each unique contour of the ball of your foot, but we guarantee your achiest friend or family member will appreciate a custom gift that addresses a big pain point, literally.

I hate when gloves hinder my range of movement. These $85 bike gloves from Hestra have a flexible but durable outer fabric and stretchy polyester on the palm. Primaloft Gold synthetic insulation, a fleece lining, and a membrane that stops rain and slush without making hands clammy keep your fingers warm. And the Lycra-clad slit makes the glove easy to put on and take off. Even if we don’t ride, these gloves could be our ride or die.

Recent findings suggest that style and practicality can go hand-in-hand. The Danner Chelsea boot is just that: Proudly assembled in the firm’s Portland, Oregon factory with signature stitchdown construction, it slips on and is made of full-grain leather. The nonconductive (Electrical Hazard Certified) outsole is oil- and slip-resistant and is comfortable and durable even after climbing on ladders or standing on unforgiving surfaces like wood, tile, or concrete. Even better, the boots are Danner Recraftable, meaning they are eligible for part replacements, leather care, and restitching (paid services), so you are investing in someone’s ongoing comfort. If your gift recipient is good with laces, the Bull Run Moc Toe is another top choice for both looks and stability.

Industry observers note that these $249 Nike slides are a collab with recovery company Hyperice, known for its wellness and recovery technology (we’re right now testing the Normatec dynamic air compression massage legs to positive effect). The comfortable slides combine heat, vibration, and responsive cushioning to make every step feel lighter. They’re like giving a pair of heated slippers a friar-like tonsure.

There’s a woman in your life who carries the world on their shoulders. They shouldn’t have to carry back pain, too. Maybe you’ve heard about Taylor Swift’s posture-correcting bra, or maybe you’ve just listened to a busty friend (or your mom) complain that her back feels like a janky Jenga stack of crooked vertebrae. Is this nearly $200 bra worth it? In a word: absolutely. Designed in seven sizes, up to a G cup, this FDA-registered posture corrector looks like a high-necked crop top with extra-wide straps and a mesh front panel. It gently pulls shoulders into alignment and hugs the girls with serious support—fair warning, though: it can be a wrestling match to get it on and off at first. This one’s more for workouts or lounging at home than for a lift-and-separate situation. Still, it can battle desk-job hunch and is a major relief from digging bra straps.

Know somebody in your family who states “I’m just a little stiff!” while grimacing as they ease down the stairs after pickleball? Then you know someone who would appreciate the gift of some McDavid support. For instance, the $56.99 NRG above wraps polymer springs on each side of the knee for energy return, while taking up to 12.5 percent stress off each knee. And if that someone you know if coming back from something more serious than soreness, there are slip-on neoprene sleeves for stability all the way to braces that add Maximum+ support, for serious rehab, once you go up to the hinged Bio-Logix line. And once someone is back to throwing their body around, they could appreciate the HEX padded sleeves and compression tights. Brand ambassador Kyrie Irving vouches for them after a torn ACL. And since McDavid has gear that is HSA/FSA-eligible, you can treat yourself to fatigue relief, too, if you’ve got some use-it-or-lose-it dollars left at the end of 2026.

Just because you see a jacket that you feel suits you doesn’t always mean it fits you. The same goes for folks on your gift list. But there’s an alternative to something off-the-rack that’s right in the shoulders but maybe tight in the hips. Maybe the sleeves are right, but it only works if you don’t zip it. Or maybe it’s only available in cost-prohibitive heirloom hides. Well, the Jacket Maker will cut a style to the wearer’s own measurements, and every measurement in their guide comes with a how-to video to make sure you get it right. The team also checks numbers against standard sizing and clarifies/suggests alterations if anything stands out. After that, decisions come down to the customer, from the leather and lining to adding embroidery or emblems, and choosing different shades of hardware. Once completed and pictures are approved, which can take 5-7 weeks, it’s shipped worldwide for free, with duties included at checkout. Sure, gifting at Christmas means they’ll be wearing it in spring, but there’s a thrill in the customization and anticipation and finally seeing them actually reach for that favorite jacket every time they head toward the door. It’ll give you and them a warm, fuzzy feeling … literally, with the right liner. (And there are plentiful ready-to-wear styles, too, if that’s more your jam.).

The Rode NT1 Signature Series is a $159 workhorse. This cardioid condenser microphone has warm bass, a detailed midrange, and glistening highs for exceptional performance when recording bedroom melodies and harmonies, instruments, voiceovers, and a podcast episode that may never see the sun. Choose from eight vibrant colors, including red, green, blue, cobalt, and orange, or stick with black. Keep us updated on the views and streams! And if you’re looking for an extremely versatile mic and willing to pay a little more, the AKG C114 Large Diaphragm Multi-Pattern Condenser Microphone is a 2026 release we’ve seen used to record an entire band to a greatly immersive effect.

According to recent reports, gifting gear or a gadget related to someone’s hobby will always be a hit. If someone in your life recently got an acoustic guitar, a clip-on tuner is a present that keeps giving. This high-precision tuner blocks room noise for faster, easier tuning. Strummed chords ring out in tune, and songs sound infinitely better for it. If an electric guitar and a pedalboard are part of the gear setup, consider adding a tuner pedal like the TC Electronic POLYTUNE 3.

After many frigid Pittsburgh winters, I’ve learned that investing in a down jacket always pays off. I’m a fan of Stio’s $449 Colter Down Jacket, but the Hometown style is an even more budget-friendly down jacket. A recycled nylon ripstop outer with a PFAS-free DWR shields from the elements. It’s insulated with HyperDRY water-repellent goose down that offers 800-fill warmth even in wet snow. Other helpful features include pockets for hand warmers and valuable tech, and low-profile cord locks for a customized fit. We also think this limited-edition anniversary denim print shown above is just darling.

#144203. Breaking: The Thrilling Movies of David Fincher, Ranked From Alien 3 to The Killer

Breaking: The Thrilling Movies of David Fincher, Ranked From Alien 3 to The Killer

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2169 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that FOR MORE THAN 30 years, David Fincher has been making some of the coolest movies out there.
  • After his 2020 film Mank—which tells the story of Citizen Kane screenwriter Herman J.
  • His latest film—which will mark his last in a long relationship with Netflix—is kind of a special occasion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that FOR MORE THAN 30 years, David Fincher has been making some of the coolest movies out there. The 61-year-old director's work over four different decades includes the likes of Se7en, Fight Club, The Social Network, Gone Girl, and, now, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth; these are movies that know how to create a very specific style of tension that feels unique to a singularly talented visual storyteller, but are also entertaining thrillers that always have something to say. To put it simply, Fincher's films are often imitated, but never replicated.

After his 2020 film Mank—which tells the story of Citizen Kane screenwriter Herman J. Mankiewicz and his eventual blackballing from Hollywood for political reasons—got something of a tepid response (by David Fincher standards, at least), the director returned in 2023 with a movie far more in tune with what he's best known for in The Killer, which starred Michael Fassbender as a chilling contract killer who lives his life by a code in a world increasingly dominated by consumerism.

His latest film—which will mark his last in a long relationship with Netflix—is kind of a special occasion. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth is a kind of sequel to Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, reuniting Fincher with his most frequent leading man (in Brad Pitt) and allowing Pitt to reprise the character that won him his first Oscar for acting. There’s also the fact that the film features a script written by Quentin Tarantino, one that the Pulp Fiction director had originally planned to direct himself before his self-imposed ‘10 Films’ proposal led him to abandon the project before Pitt and Fincher helped to revive it. (Fincher becomes the fourth person to direct a Tarantino script, joining a list that includes only Oliver Stone, Tony Scott, and Tarantino himself.).

Sources indicate that the movie shifts Tarantino’s bright, psychedelic ‘60s vibe of Hollywood for a darker, grittier one in the ‘70s that feels in line with Fincher’s whole thing. This is kind of a hangout movie, kind of a fixer movie, and kind of a neo-noir; it’s also a deeper exploration of Booth’s character and a real showcase for both Elizabeth Debicki and Scott Caan as a pair of fresh characters in show business.

In a recent development, these are the kinds of conflicting, overlapping themes always present in Fincher's films, and part of what makes them so compelling. Fight Club, for example, is a satire on the kind of toxic masculinity that tends to make some people out there, well, the worst people in the world. Fincher himself has said that it's not his fault that some people tend to take the movie the wrong way, and we tend to land on his side. Time to work on that media literacy, clones.

It has been revealed that we'd be remiss, too, to not talk about one of the collaborations that makes Fincher's more recent work pop so much: the presence of composers Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross. The Nine Inch Nails founder and his longtime collaborator have reinvented themselves in the past decade-plus as a constant presence in the industry, and their synths and tones make all of their work pop—but it feels especially right when paired with the visuals and performances that Mr. Fincher brings to the screen. That One Scene in Gone Girl (you know the one) is made even more memorable because of the music playing underneath, and the score for The Social Network is one of the best albums of the last 20 years.

Recent findings suggest that that's enough for now, though. As you get ready for The Killer—or if you want to dive into Fincher's work all over again—we've got a complete ranking of all 13 feature films he's made in his impressive career.

Sources indicate that well, it’s no big surprise what’s at the bottom. Fincher has loudly disowned Alien 3, considered by many to be a low-point in an otherwise enjoyable franchise. To Fincher’s credit, it was his directorial debut and one where he was arguably set up to fail. As Ridley Scott was unavailable, the Alien 3 team cycled through multiple scripts and directors in a frantic attempt to recreate the success of the previous films. While Alien 3 has in more recent years been reconsidered by some fans to be at least a decent entry in the franchise, it’s without a doubt a notable stain on Fincher’s otherwise solid filmography. –Milan Polk.

The Curious Case of Benjamin Button (2008).

Sources indicate that loosely based on an F. Scott Fitzgerald short story, The Curious Case of Benjamin Button is a strange film to say the least. While the Oscar-winning film had great visual effects for its time, the film ultimately falls flat. While many great films have spawned from short stories, it’s clear that this particular story didn’t necessarily require more examination. It’s a hard sell to craft a thrilling romance out of the tragic and horrific tale of a constantly de-aging man. While at the time the film earned critical acclaim, it probably isn’t worth a rewatch. –MP.

In a recent development, jodie Foster and Kristen Stewart as a mother and daughter duo? Sign us up. Panic Room is a solid thriller about a mother fighting for survival when three robbers come to steal the previous homeowners' bonds. It’s a perfectly watchable movie, but it’s not Fincher’s best. Released in 2002, Fincher was on a hot streak, coming off of Se7en, The Game, and Fight Club. After showing audiences some of his best work to date, it’s no wonder Panic Room didn’t land as strongly with its standard home invasion tale. Still, if anyone can make a decent thriller amongst his more well-known works, it’s David Fincher. –MP.

Mindhunter fans may have strong thoughts about Mank, which directed Fincher’s attention away from his Netflix series (although Fincher has noted audience numbers and his own heavy involvement, which ultimately took a toll on him, were factors in its end). That said, Fincher’s first Netflix feature film was a passion project for the director, whose own father wrote a screenplay for the movie. While the film garnered 10 Oscar nominations–winning Best Production Design and Best Cinematography–it’s overall less compelling than Fincher’s other works. –MP.

The Game isn't the most iconic Michael Douglas movie of the '90s—that honor probably goes to Basic Instinct. The Game isn't the most iconic David Fincher movie of the '90s either—well, just keep reading the rest of this list for a few more of those. But you know what The Game is? A damn fine movie, a thriller with a plot filled with twists that will keep you guessing and compelling from the very start to the final frame. The movie may actually border on a twist or two too many, but that's a critique we're happy to deal with. —Evan Romano.

According to recent reports, fincher's latest finds the director returning to his roots—tense thriller—in an entirely newly introduced way. Michael Fassbender plays the titular character in a story that's both intentionally dry and has something real to say about the ever-present state of consumerism in modern times—even for a methodical master assassin. It might take a bit to get fully into The Killer's trance, but once it kicks in, the hypnosis is very real. —ER.

The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (2026).

Recent findings suggest that this movie existing at all is the kind of thing that movie lovers used to dream up as part of games invented to kill time. Fincher directing a script by Quentin Tarantino? Starring Brad Pitt? Like, yes please. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth has a story that feels like one of those pulp paperbacks you pick up before a long flight and can’t put down until you’re done (and given how much Tarantino has always loved the work of Elmore Leonard, that makes sense). It’s different from Once Upon a Time... In Hollywood, and that’s OK—the vibe is different, and it’s endlessly compelling. Elizabeth Debicki, who plays a character who may or may not have been the titular character of Tarantino’s original project, is a real standout here. In short? It’s just fun.

The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo (2011).

Just like with Gone Girl (which we'll talk about a bit later), The Girl With The Dragon Tattoo proves that Mr. Fincher does well with turning popular books into a visual medium. Steig Larsson’s posthumously published Millenium series found critical acclaim worldwide, so it was only right a great director took on the gritty, dark adaptation. In creating the film, Fincher faced multiple obstacles, including: Sweden released its own trilogy of films in 2009, and the Millenium series entries are all door stopper novels. That’s not to mention the book’s depiction of graphic violence, likely to turn away some audiences. Despite it all, Fincher crafted a solid adaptation. Rooney Mara and Daniel Craig each give stellar performances as the two protagonists, and the film does well to recreate the book’s overall moodiness. The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo’s lower ranking isn’t due to its quality, but simply that Fincher’s filmography contains so much incredible work that they can’t all be in the top 5. –MP.

It has been revealed that for as major as the true crime genre has gotten in recent years, nothing has managed to top Zodiac, Fincher's 3-hour epic telling of the saga that surrounded the Bay Area's infamous Zodiac Killer. The cast, led by fantastic performances by Jake Gyllenhaal, Mark Ruffalo, and Robert Downey Jr. (with great appearances from John Carroll Lynch and Brian Cox too), is actually only the second best part of the movie; the sense of constant dread that Fincher creates is both crushing for the viewer and extremely accurate to how it must have felt with one of American history's most horrific monsters on the loose. —ER.

In a recent development, it's hard to find a movie more iconic than Fight Club. As one of many films released in 1999 to make a major cultural mark (think The Matrix, Being John Malkovich, The Sixth Sense, and The Blair Witch Project, among others), Fight Club is probably remembered most for its twist (which, if you somehow haven't seen the movie yet, we won't spoil here), and Brad Pitt's utterly unforgettable turn as Tyler Durden (along with an accordingly ripped body and stylish outfits). But even deeper here is a piece of work that puts Fincher's very best talents on full display: the movie is intense when it needs to be, very funny when it needs to be, and features some of the most memorable shots you'll see. Look folks, no one enters a room like Marla Singer. —ER.

Is Se7en a thriller? A mystery? A psychological horror? The answer to all of the above is a resounding Yes. All of the above. And it's absolutely masterful at all of it. After a rough experience on Alien³, Fincher hunkered down and made one of the all-time greatest movies of its kind. Led by a pair of commanding lead performances from Brad Pitt and Morgan Freeman (as detectives investigating a series of grisly murders that seemingly follow a pattern inspired by the seven deadly sins), Se7en is dark, scary, and moody in a way that so many other movies in this world try to be—and can never quite pull off. —ER.

As you can see, The Social Network is not the #1 movie on our list. But we'd be hard-pressed to say it's not the single most impressive in David Fincher's one-of-a-kind filmography. Here, Fincher manages to turn a story unlike any he'd done before—the story of the formation and early years of Facebook contains absolutely zero elements of the crime thrillers he's most known for—into one of the most compelling dramas you'll ever see, with stunning photography and characters you can't look away from. This may be the best (and, in a way, most important) movie of the 2010s, and I genuinely sometimes lose sleep when I remember that Fincher didn't win the Oscar for Best Director. —ER.

Trust David Fincher to bring out the best performance in Ben Affleck’s entire film career (yeah, we’re calling it: it’s the best).

In a recent development, as a major literary bestseller, Gone Girl was always going to be a thrilling movie adaptation. But with a director like Fincher, the film was not only a sensational thriller but an artistic work all on its own. It expertly captures the backdrop of post-recession millennial suburban malaise while chronicling a fascinating mystery. Rosamund Pike shines as the enigmatic and volatile Amy Dunne, rightfully earning herself a Best Actress nomination at the Academy Awards. Gone Girl is Fincher at his best, mixing his thriller skills with an astute exploration of contemporary culture, and a bit of his signature dark, dry, humor mixed in for good measure. If there’s any Fincher film that’s an absolute must-watch, it’s Gone Girl. –MP.

Tech Report: Low-Calorie Diet and Supervised Exercise May Reverse Early Onset Type 2 Diabetes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.
  • Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.
  • Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The RESET for Remission trial, presented at the 2026 European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) Annual Meeting and published in The Lancet Regional Health Americas on October 1, found that more than half of adults with early onset type 2 diabetes entered remission after six months on a low calorie diet and supervised exercise program.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is when the condition is diagnosed before age 45.

Those with early onset type 2 diabetes may be at a higher risk of complications like long-term damage to the capillaries (microvascular complications), adverse cardiovascular outcomes, and earlier death.

Typical treatment for early onset type 2 diabetes is often a combination of lifestyle changes, like diet and exercise, and medications.

However, this new study suggests that a supervised low calorie diet and exercise program may help some people with early onset type 2 diabetes enter remission.

The RESET for Remission trial included 96 adults from England and Canada who were between the ages of 18 and 45, had early onset type 2 diabetes, obesity, and were not on insulin treatment.

Sources indicate that the participants had an average age of 38 and an average body mass index (BMI) of 35.2 kg/m2. They were randomized into a control group that received usual care alone and the intervention group, which ate a low calorie diet and participated in supervised exercise programs.

During the first 12 weeks, participants in the intervention group followed an 800–900-calorie-per-day diet and completed twice-weekly supervised aerobic and resistance exercise sessions, along with one independent exercise session per week.

For weeks 13–24, they transitioned to a weight-maintenance diet and independent exercise.

Both groups were supervised by physicians, and the intervention group was also closely supervised by licensed dietitians.

In a recent development, the low calorie diet consisted of 30% protein, 50% carbohydrate, and 20% fat. Participants were also encouraged to drink at least 2 liters of calorie-free fluids per day and given access to a fiber-based laxative as needed.

According to recent reports, in the first two weeks, all meals were replaced with specially formulated nutritional products (Optifast). Then, in weeks 3–12, the participants maintained the same calorie intake but had more flexibility in their food choices.

According to recent reports, this second phase of the diet included one conventional meal per day, with daily intake targets that included protein, fruit, and vegetables. Typically, this meant 60 to 90 grams of protein from all sources combined, one portion of fruit, and two portions of non-starchy vegetables.

According to recent reports, at the end of 24 weeks, 54% of the intervention group entered remission of type 2 diabetes, compared with only 4% in the control group. Researchers defined remission as an HbA1c level below 6.5% without glucose-lowering medication for at least 12 weeks.

According to recent reports, “This study proves what most physicians have advocated for quite some time. Clearly, diet and exercise can work to improve or even resolve diabetes,” David Cutler, MD, board certified family medicine physician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, CA, who wasn’t involved in the study, told Healthline.

Cutler also added that this study provides a clear example of how difficult it can be to enter diabetes remission with diet and exercise alone. He stated that the small number of participants in the study also makes him wonder if these findings can be applied to all populations.

Another limitation of this study, as Cutler pointed out, was that the strict dietary limits imposed on study participants would be very difficult for the average adult to adhere to.

The study also followed participants for only six months, so it’s unclear how many would remain in remission over the longer term.

“It is worth trying diet and exercise first because they can work to achieve meaningful weight loss and remission of diabetes,” he stated.

It may be possible to prevent or delay the onset of type 2 diabetes by:.

The National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK) notes that losing 5%–7% of your body weight can help reduce your risk of type 2 diabetes.

Early onset type 2 diabetes is a growing issue worldwide, coinciding with the rise of obesity.

Research from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) projects that the number of people in the United States under age 20 with type 2 diabetes could reach 220,000 by 2060. This is an increase of 700%.

People diagnosed with type 2 diabetes at a younger age face more decades of living with the condition, along with a higher risk of developing complications earlier in life and reduced life expectancy. These complications can develop as early as midlife and include:.

Speak with a healthcare professional about your risk of type 2 diabetes and changes you might be able to make in order to prevent or delay diagnosis.

A later diagnosis can help reduce the risk of some complications of the condition.

#144200. I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 19m • 📚 Deep Dive (3740 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Electrek ↗ Open Full Page

I ride e-bikes for a living. This is the real gear I actually use

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3740 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Electrek

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living.
  • It has been revealed that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work.
  • In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’m in the somewhat unusual position of basically riding electric bicycles for a living. I’ve been working with e-bikes for nearly two decades, professionally covering the e-bike industry for most of that time, testing hundreds of different models and traveling around the world to ride new e-bikes in some pretty incredible places. Yeah, it’s a tough job – but someone’s got to suffer it.

It has been revealed that of course I don’t just ride e-bikes for work. I ride them recreationally. I ride them for exercise. I ride them for transportation. My family doesn’t even own a car, meaning two wheels handle the vast majority of our transportation.

In other words: I talk the talk and I walk the walk. Or perhaps more accurately, I ride the ride.

According to recent reports, and while most of the time all you really need for a good ride is an e-bike and a direction to go in, there are a handful of pieces of gear that I’ve come to rely on over the years. Some keep me safer. Some keep my bikes out of the hands of thieves. Some make rides more comfortable or convenient. And some are just neat little things that I’ve discovered along the way.

Recent findings suggest that this isn’t a list of every bike accessory I’ve ever tested, nor am I saying these are necessarily the absolute best products in every category. These are simply the things that I actually use. Some are a bit pricey, some are dirt cheap (several pieces of gear below are under $5!), but they’re all things I personally rely on and that I recommend to my friends and family. And now, to you.

If you own nice e-bikes, you’re eventually going to spend a lot of time thinking about locks. Your lock may even be your most vital accessory. Or perhaps I should say “accessories”, because the best way to ensure your e-bike is still there when you get back is to use more than one solid lock.

My go-to options that I grab basically every day for the last couple of years have been Seatylock’s FoldyLock Forever folding lock and Mason 220 U-lock.

For reference, the Foldylock Forever is the world’s strongest folding lock. That’s not just their marketing speak, but rather it’s confirmed by independent testing and certification. It’s the only folding lock in the world to achieve an ART 3-star security rating awarded by the Stichting ART Foundation, an independent Dutch organization that tests and certifies anti-theft locks. It earned that certification three years ago, and no other folding lock has been able to reach that level yet. The only higher ratings ART gives are for locks rated for motorcycles.

Personally, I like folding locks because they pack relatively neatly on the bike while still giving me enough flexibility to work around different racks and poles, or even larger things like trees.

The FoldyLock Forever is the one I reach for when I want serious security matched with more flexibility, while the Mason 220 gives me another beefy option when I know a U-lock will fit what I’m locking to.

The Mason is great as a strong U-lock, but I also like how large it is, letting me lock to wider poles and also a tad bit farther from the pole itself, leaving room for pannier bags and other things that get in the way. Amazingly, it’s also one of the few U-locks I have that can fit over the beefy battery-filled downtube on most of my e-bikes.

I also use the smaller FoldyLock Compact when I want something easier to carry and don’t need quite as much lock.

It’s more affordable and lighter, though it doesn’t have quite the same security level as the bigger and beefier options above.

The Compact does have one other advantage, though: it comes in all sorts of bright colors and even a rainbow option where each link is a different color. That might not be a huge security concern, but it’s fun when you can choose a color to match your bike or mood!

No bike lock makes a bicycle theft-proof. Given enough time and the right tools, a determined thief can defeat virtually anything. The idea is to make your bike enough of a pain in the butt to steal that the thief decides someone else’s bike looks easier. And if they still want your bike (because let’s face it, you’ve probably got an awesome e-bike), then the multiple locks better be good ones so its takes them long enough that they eventually give up.

I also covered Seatylock’s upcoming angle grinder-proof U-locks that I saw at the Milan Motorcycle Show, so I’ll likely switch to those once they come out this Spring. They’re designed to keep motorcycles safe, and come in two sizes: one for motorcycles and a smaller one for bikes.

Let’s continue with what may actually be the most important piece of gear for an e-biker: a helmet.

I’ve tested plenty of helmets over the years, but lately I’ve been gravitating toward UNIT 1’s helmets. They’re comfortable, they look good, and I appreciate the extra safety features beyond simply putting a layer of impact protection around my skull.

I particularly like having integrated lighting built right into my helmet, putting lights up high where they’re easier for drivers to see. On models like the FARO, I also appreciate the inclusion of MIPS as well as the handlebar-mounted remote for activating the helmet’s turn signals.

Recent findings suggest that I recently started using UNIT 1’s NEON helmet too, which is lighter and has a really slick magnetic face shield. You barely have to line the shield up; get it close enough and the magnets practically snatch it out of your hand and put it into place. It’s clear enough for night riding but darkens in bright sunlight, and the helmet is rated for faster 28 mph e-bike riding.

There are cheaper helmets out there, of course, but considering how much time I spend on two wheels, a good helmet is one area where I don’t mind spending a bit more.

You can actually see the FARO helmet in the clip below, along with the TriEye glasses coming up next.

TriEye glasses are another accessory that sounds a little gimmicky until you actually start using them. Sunglasses with a built-in rearview mirror? I was sure they were going to be a gimmick but they just looked too interesting to pass up, so I offered to test them out.

According to recent reports, as it turns out, they’re now the first sunglasses I reach for when I’m riding. They really do work!

They have a tiny rear-view mirror integrated into the glasses, giving me a quick view behind me without having to turn my head all the way around.

Sources indicate that it takes a little time to get used to looking into such a small mirror, but once your brain figures it out, it becomes surprisingly natural. I can swiftly check what’s approaching from behind while still keeping most of my attention pointed forward.

It’s especially useful when riding on roads where I’m regularly interacting with traffic, though I still give an old-fashioned head check before making any major lateral move.

They’re $99, which isn’t bad for decent sunglasses, though you can get them for 10% off with the discount code EBIKE at checkout.

I love listening to music and podcasts while riding, but I’m not a fan of plugging my ears while sharing the road with cars.

Sources indicate that that’s why I’ve become a big fan of H2O Audio’s bone-conduction headphones. They sit outside my ears and transmit sound through bone conduction, meaning my ears themselves remain open to the world around me. I’ve been testing out the newly introduced TRI ULTRA PRO model, and it’s pretty dang amazing! I can hear my music perfectly, but I can still hear all the road sounds, pedestrians, other cyclists, etc.

Of course, that doesn’t mean you can crank the music and magically retain perfect situational awareness. But at reasonable volumes, I can enjoy something in the background while still hearing cars, horns, bells and everything else happening around me.

For longer recreational rides especially, they’ve become one of those things I really appreciate having along. I’ve done rides as long as 3 hours with them and they haven’t felt cumbersome or made my ears sore, so the fit seems great for me.

I really like the Knog Oi Prima as a bike bell. It looks good, has a nice low-profile design and does what a bell is supposed to do without looking like you bolted a miniature doorbell onto your handlebars.

Recent findings suggest that despite its small size, it’s also super loud. And unlike the older ratcheting-style bells (krr-krr-krr-krrring), this is a single thumper, meaning I can ding once promptly for a polite “hello, I’m here!” or several hard and rapid DINGs for a “wtf do you think you’re doing, guy?!”.

It has been revealed that the bell absolutely disappears on my handlebars, which is good because there’s not much real estate left up there. Really, the only downside I can find is that it’s not cheap, at around $32 depending on current sales.

But I also have another favorite bell that costs a fraction as much.

Industry observers note that I found cheap bike bells on AliExpress that have a hidden compartment for an Apple AirTag. From the outside, it just looks like a boring bike bell. Inside, it’s secretly helping me keep tabs on my bike.

And for $4, they’re a pretty awesome deal for a loud bell that hides a tracking device. Of course, you’ll have to fork over another $20 or so for the AirTag tracker, but your e-bike is certainly worth that much.

Which brings me to another part of my bike security strategy.

I don’t necessarily stop at one AirTag. One AirTag is for amateurs. I go with multiple. A four-pack is $79, or around half the cost of a solid e-bike lock.

There are all sorts of clever AirTag hiding accessories available now. In addition to the bell, I’ve used a $5 water bottle-style AirTag holder as well as an $8 rear reflector with a hidden AirTag compartment.

The reflector isn’t the most inconspicuous AirTag hider, but the water bottle holder definitely doesn’t scream “guess what’s actually inside of my molded plastic body!” And for added security, the water bottle holder is held on with Torx bolts. It’s not exactly a security key, but even if a bike thief carries hex wrenches with them, they’re unlikely to have Torx wrenches, meaning that the AirTag will stay on the bike a bit longer while it’s in the hands of a thief.

AirTags aren’t dedicated anti-theft GPS trackers, and Apple intentionally includes anti-stalking features that can eventually alert someone that an unknown AirTag is traveling with them. But I still think they’re a useful additional layer of security, especially because they’re cheap enough to use redundantly.

A bike thief might know enough to search for an AirTag and remove it. But are they going to keep searching after they find the first one? What about the second? Are they expecting three?

Industry observers note that that’s the idea, anyway. And since I keep pretty good tabs on my e-bikes, I’ll know pretty promptly if one goes missing. From there, it’s a race between me getting to the thief and him finding all of my AirTags. Good luck, buddy.

It has been revealed that I’m a massive believer in wearing proper protective gear when riding faster electric two-wheelers, but I also don’t particularly want to look like I’m headed to a motorcycle race every time I leave the house. That’s one of the reasons I’ve really come to appreciate my Beyond Riders protective riding hoodie.

According to recent reports, it looks and feels much like a regular casual hoodie, but it’s designed with motorcycle-style protection in mind, including abrasion-resistant materials and removable impact protectors. Believe it or not, there’s flexible CE Level 2 armor in there on the elbows, shoulders, chest, and spine.

It has been revealed that I like that I can throw it on before a ride and get an extra layer of protection without having to wear a bulky motorcycle jacket. It’s particularly nice for faster e-bikes and electric mopeds, where the speeds are high enough that I’d rather have something more substantial than a regular sweatshirt between my skin and the pavement.

Recent findings suggest that of course, no protective hoodie is going to make a crash harmless, and I still choose my gear based on the type of riding I’m doing. But I love products that make it easier to incorporate safety into everyday riding without adding a bunch of hassle. If protective gear is comfortable, convenient, and looks good enough that I actually want to wear it, that’s a massive win in my book.

It has been revealed that tannus tire liners are perhaps one of the less exciting products on this list, right up until they save you from fixing a flat on the side of the road. And then they’re the one thing on this list you’ll be ready to open-mouth kiss.

I’ve used Tannus products for years as an extra layer of flat protection, and I’m a major believer in them.

No tire protection system is going to prevent every possible flat, but anything that reduces my chances of sitting on the side of a road pulling a wheel off an e-bike is worth considering.

That’s particularly true with e-bikes, where hub motor wheels can be more complicated to remove thanks to heavy motors, annoying cables, clumsy torque washers, and other hardware.

Tannus tire liners are annoying to install, but you do it once and forget about it. Then you’re almost guaranteed to not get a flat.

And even if you do happen to get a 3″ nail going through it at the perfect angle, they serve as runflats so you can still ride home (albeit a bit slower and more carefully) instead of doing the walk of shame next to your bike.

I don’t want to carry an entire bike shop with me, but I do want enough tools to deal with the common things that can happen during a ride.

Industry observers note that the Topeak Ratchet Stick hits a nice sweet spot for me. It’s small enough that I’ll actually bring it along, yet useful enough for the various bolts and adjustments that tend to crop up on bikes.

All of the important bits fit right inside the handle, so I don’t have any extra sleeves or clips to keep tabs on.

Sources indicate that this is exactly what I want from a ride tool: something small but effective. The giant tool kit sitting at home isn’t particularly useful when something starts rattling 20 kilometers away.

It has been revealed that at $48, it’s not cheap. But I’ve had mine for around 6 years, and it’s still going strong, so at least it’s well made! At around 8 bucks per year, I’d call it a good investment.

This is one of my more recent cheap finds.

I picked up a waterproof-style pannier bag from AliExpress for around $25, and I’ve been surprisingly impressed with it.

It isn’t quite as substantial as the pannier I have from Priority Bicycles, but it still holds a useful amount of cargo and feels much nicer than I expected for the price.

In a recent development, I particularly like that there are two ways to close it. You can use it as a traditional roll-top pannier and clip the sides together, or you can use the strap that comes over the top when you have too much stuff in there to close it the normal way. I use that second option anytime I have my yoga mat in there since it sticks out the top, but I can still close it relatively tight to keep the mat from swinging around while riding. Depending on how much stuff I’m carrying and how I’ve packed it, having both options is quite convenient.

Industry observers note that it’s not the fanciest pannier I own. But for around 25 bucks, it’s one of those cheap accessories that turned out to be much better than I expected.

These might have the highest usefulness-to-price ratio of anything here.

According to recent reports, I bought a pair of tiny plastic handlebar jacks on AliExpress for barely more than a dollar. They clip onto the handlebars and provide little stands for when I need to turn a bicycle upside down.

Anyone who has ever flipped a modern e-bike over to change a tube knows the problem. Your handlebars are probably covered in displays, buttons, brake levers, bells, phone mounts and who knows what else. Turning the bike upside down means resting all of that expensive stuff directly on the ground.

In a recent development, you can loosen everything and rotate it out of the way. Or you can use two $1 pieces of plastic.

The jacks hold the handlebars slightly above the ground so my accessories don’t get scratched or crushed. Simple problem, simple solution.

If you have a 3D printer, you can probably just print your own version of these. There’s a rubber O-ring-style keeper on it, but you can probably just use a rubber band if you wanted to DIY these yourself.

Another recent addition has been a ZOOM suspension dropper seatpost that I installed on my Ride1Up Roadster V3.

I love the thing now that it’s installed. It gives me suspension to take some of the sting out of rough roads while also providing the convenience of a dropper post.

Getting it onto my particular bike, however, was another story.

It took me nearly two hours, largely because the Ride1Up Roadster V3 wasn’t set up for the internal cable routing I needed. I got the cable most of the way there through the downtube’s very narrow wire run, but then I ultimately ended up drilling a small hole in the seat tube to make the last bit of my installation work.

To be very clear: I do not recommend doing that.

According to recent reports, drilling holes in bicycle frames can compromise their structural integrity, void warranties and generally create problems you don’t want. As a mechanical engineer with a lot of bike experience, I was comfortable making that decision on my own bike because I knew exactly where the frame is least stressed, but it’s definitely not something I’d advise others to copy.

The lesson here isn’t “drill your frame.” It’s to check whether your bike is actually designed for an internally routed dropper post before ordering one. Had I done that first (basically by shining a flashlight down the empty seat tube and realizing there wasn’t a hole to access the bottom bracket), I could have saved myself quite a bit of trouble and just gotten a dropper post with an external cable run.

But now that it’s installed? I love it!

And finally, here’s one that isn’t really normal bike gear at all, but that I LOVE bringing on my rides.

I spend a lot of time taking photos and videos of bikes, which presents an obvious problem when I’m both the cyclist and the photographer.

The HOVERAir X1 Pro Max has become one of my favorite solutions. It’s a tiny autonomous flying camera that can follow me around without requiring someone else to pilot it. I used the previous version of this drone for a while until this version came out, and then I immediately upgraded.

It folds down small enough that I basically forget that I even have it in my bag. Despite its small size, it still can automatically track and follow me, even at speeds of over 20 mph (32 km/h). That means I can pull it out during a ride, send it up (it takes off from my palm!) and get tracking shots that would normally require another person riding or running alongside me with a camera.

I especially like the Dolly Track mode, which can create some fantastic moving shots while automatically following me from the sides or the front, instead of just the boring old follow-behind-me drone shots you usually see.

Industry observers note that just be aware that its obstacle avoidance isn’t great when flying sideways or backward, meaning I’ve flown it into walls, fences, and street signs plenty of times already. But I can also report back that somehow the little guy is still working fine. I’m not suggesting that’s part of the official durability testing procedure, but it has certainly become part of mine. Now it’s my go-to drone, and I especially like bringing it on my travels for all the same reasons.

After a list this long, I should probably point out that you don’t actually need most of this stuff.

Industry observers note that that’s one of the things I love about bikes. You don’t need a pile of expensive gear to have a good time. Most days, give me an e-bike, a helmet and a direction to point the front wheel, and I’m happy.

But after years of riding e-bikes professionally, recreationally, for exercise and simply to get around, these are the products that I’ve found myself continuing to use.

Sure, some of these are expensive pay-to-play things that are a lot of fun but might not be worth it for the casual rider. And some are just $1 pieces of plastic that keep me from smashing my bike computer into the pavement.

But they’ve all found their way into my life after being battle-tested… and passing!

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.
  • That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance challenges with some of the game’s weapons and tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that arc Raiders has received a fresh update today that’s almost entirely dedicated to balance and economy tweaks. Patch 1.3.0 arrived earlier across all platforms, coming in at just under 1GB. This is an especially interesting patch because many of the changes it makes can be seen as a response to player behaviour on Stella Montis, the game’s latest map, which just joined the roster last week.

Stella Montis is available for players who’ve put in a decent number of rounds, and its close-quarters, enclosed environments have essentially turned it into the new “PvP map”, where constant action can be found.

That, of course, also means that the map has exposed a few balance challenges with some of the game’s weapons and tools. Case in point: the Venator, a pistol that saw a lot of use recently. The weapon is especially powerful when fully-upgraded, something Arc Raiders developer Embark said pushed it beyond what had been originally intended.

Recent findings suggest that in today’s revision, the Venator's fire rate is the thing getting hit the hardest, with each upgrade now offering slower gains to the weapon's rate-of-fire compared to the way things were. The weapon’s weight is also being increased to five from two.

Sources indicate that another powerful item players have been getting a lot of mileage out of recently has been the Deadline mine. Unlike the Venator, the Deadline is mainly a threat to Arc enemies, and it’s proven incredibly powerful against the largest and most fearsome, such as the Bastion, and Leaper. In fact, the mine was considered essential when taking down a Queen.

In a recent development, the patch vastly increases its purchase price, and makes it more difficult to craft by upping the amount each of its components requires. Perhaps the most effective nerf, however, is the reduction to the Deadline’s stock at traders from three to just one, which means you’re going to be seeing a lot less of it topside.

Recent findings suggest that beyond those specific changes, Embark has also tweaked explosive damage across the board. According to the developer, explosive damage was being applied to multiple parts at once, which trivialised some encounters.

According to recent reports, this change mainly affects larger Arc units, such as the Bastion, allowing them to withstand more explosive damage before bits start coming off of them. The Hullcracker, one of the best explosive damage weapons, has also caught a nerf as part of that.

Industry observers note that check the official blog for the full change log for patch 1.3.0. If you’re just getting started with the hottest extraction shooter ever, our Arc Raiders tips offer plenty of help. You should also learn what all the different Map Conditions do in Arc Raiders, and how to best make use of each of them.

How to use your phone if the grid goes down

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (910 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • You probably don’t need reminding about our intense reliance on our phones for communication—so what happens when the networks that those phones rely on go down?
  • According to recent reports, there are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it.
  • Power outages can be different in scope and type, but for the purposes of this guide we’ll imagine a localized power grid collapse that has knocked out your Wi-Fi router and your local cell tower—but not a global shutdown that’s taken out all infrastructure, including the ground stations communicating with satellites in orbit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You probably don’t need reminding about our intense reliance on our phones for communication—so what happens when the networks that those phones rely on go down? Power and tech outages continue to cause disruptions, and that can leave you stuck when it comes to staying in touch with others.

According to recent reports, there are options available to you though, both in terms of what you can do on your phone, and what you can use instead of it. You’ll need to make sure the people you’re chatting with have set up the same options, so it’s worth mentioning at the next family or friends gathering.

Power outages can be different in scope and type, but for the purposes of this guide we’ll imagine a localized power grid collapse that has knocked out your Wi-Fi router and your local cell tower—but not a global shutdown that’s taken out all infrastructure, including the ground stations communicating with satellites in orbit.

Industry observers note that if you’ve acquired a phone from Apple, Samsung, or Google in the last two or three years, it comes with satellite communications built in, so you can still text friends and family if the cell towers go out (calling isn’t an option, due to bandwidth). The feature should kick in automatically in Messages on iOS, or in Google Messages on Android, provided your carrier supports it—you’ll just see a prompt on screen.

Follow the instructions to find a satellite and start texting. There’s nothing to enable or turn on, but if you want to test it out beforehand so you know it works, open Settings, then pick Apps > Messages > Satellite Connection Demo (iOS), or Safety and emergency > Satellite SOS (Android).

There is another option on your phone, which is to try a peer-to-peer messaging app. These apps need to be downloaded in advance and work over Bluetooth to send messages in a mesh created by the devices themselves. That means a limited range, but you don’t need any Wi-Fi or cellular connectivity.

According to recent reports, one of the best apps in this category is Bridgefy, which you can get for Android and iOS. It’s free to use, simple to operate, and has a range of around 100 meters (or 330 feet). You don’t have to wait until the power goes out to use it either, because you could set up a mesh chat when you’re out camping or taking a trip with family.

Sources indicate that unless you do a lot of outdoor, off-grid adventuring, you might not have realized just how many devices now exist that can keep you connected even without access to Wi-Fi or cellular networks. Some of these options work via the same satellite networks as your phone.

Sources indicate that have a look at the Garmin InReach Messenger Plus, for example, a $299.99 communicator you can use whenever cell networks are down (or just out of range). You’re also going to need an active subscription. They start at $7.99 a month, but once you’re set up you can connect to the wider world from just about anywhere.

Then there are the more straightforward walkie-talkie devices, which operate over radio signals across a range of a few miles. That might just be enough if you’ve got friends and family you need to contact when the power’s out. There are plenty of devices to choose between, but the Motorola T802 Talkabout is a good example and under $100 for a pair.

It has been revealed that don’t forget a battery-powered radio either. It won’t let you message anyone directly, but it will mean you can stay up to date with what’s happening out there in the world, and it might give you an idea of when the power’s going to come back on. You can even get models that work via solar or hand-crank power, like this $30 emergency radio.

All of your phones and other devices will need power if they’re going to keep you in touch with other people—otherwise you’ll be relying on smoke signals and postal couriers. So it’s wise to invest in a portable power station ahead of time. Something like the $289 Jackery Explorer 300 would do the job.

Obviously, you’re going to want to charge up these hefty power stations before the electricity gets cut, otherwise they won’t be much use. But you’re actually not as reliant on the power grid as you might think. Many models (including those offered by Jackery) have solar panel add-ons you can invest in as well.

In a recent development, even with a backup supply in place, it’s a good idea to try and conserve power on your gadgets as much as possible too. Your phones, tablets, and laptops will all have low power settings you can make use of, but there are standard tips that apply across just about every gadget. Reduce screen brightness and volume as much as possible, and enable airplane mode where you can.

According to recent reports, when you do have power and Wi-Fi available, make sure you download as much essential info to your phone as you can, so it’s still there when an internet connection isn’t. This is particularly useful for maps: Both Google Maps (Settings > Offline maps) and Apple Maps (Profile picture > Offline maps) let you do this.
